name: Rafael Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run two CNC lathes at a car parts plant on the old airfield, turning brake discs. CNC means the machine is computer controlled: I load the rough castings, start the program, check the finished discs with a gauge and swap the cutting tips when they wear. Most of the job is watching numbers and listening, and when an alarm code comes up I'm still the guy who has to look it up. I love the moment a disc comes out shiny and true, and I hate the night shifts, because my body never gets used to them.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said you look up alarm codes. How do you do that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Honestly, I ask a chatbot on my phone, every day, and then check with Yusuf, the setter, before I touch anything. I've only been doing this two years. Before that I worked in bars and played bass in a covers band, until my partner Sofia and I had Nico, who's ten now, and Clara, who's seven, and the late nights stopped making sense. Sofia works the counter at a bakery, and between us we earn enough for the mortgage and food, and that's it, there's nothing left over at the end of the month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Funny, because AI is already the most useful tool I've got, and it's still a tool. So that sounds a bit like now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say look, it helps, it's not magic, stop panicking and stop selling it as a miracle. And I'd say the real question was never the AI, it's who gets the savings, because the plant still made record profits last year and we got two percent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's fine, maybe a little bit good. I'd keep using the chatbot to learn faster than the guys who won't, and maybe in a couple of years I'm a setter like Yusuf. That's more money, which we need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep using it to learn the machines, ask for the setter training, and keep at it. I'd probably get the young guy on my shift, Theo, using it too, he's scared of breaking things. Nothing big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Normal life, a bit of hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned record profits and two percent. Does that bother you more than the technology?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Much more. The technology is just a hammer. What bothers me is who holds it. In the canteen we all know exactly how much the new building cost and how little the raise was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would setter money change at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd mean when the washing machine breaks, it's annoying instead of a disaster. That's it. That's the dream, a broken washing machine that's just annoying.

S0.say: AI helps, but it's not magic, so stop panicking and stop selling it as a miracle. The real question is who gets the savings, because the plant made record profits and we got two percent.
S0.think: For me the slow version is fine, maybe a little good, because I use AI to learn faster than the guys who won't. In a couple of years I might be a setter, and we need that money.
S0.do: Keeps using the chatbot to learn the machines and asks for setter training. Helps a younger colleague start using AI tools too.
S0.feel: Calm, with a bit of hope.
S0.quote: That's the dream, a broken washing machine that's just annoying.
S0.fieldNote: Rafael already treats AI as a daily learning tool and sees it as a way to climb faster despite being junior. His anger is about how profits are shared, not the technology. His dream is modest and precise: enough slack that a breakdown isn't a crisis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is the one I actually think is happening. You can see it already, they're putting robot loaders on lathes in the other hall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the robots are coming and the question is whether workers get trained to run them or get thrown out. Unions should be demanding training budgets and a share of the gains. I'd say that in the union meeting and online, and I'd say it to the managers too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately? I think this one could be good for me if I move fast. Someone has to program and look after the robot loaders, and I'm the guy already asking the chatbot how robot cells work at two in the morning. The risk is that the company hires a technician from outside instead of training someone like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the robotics maintenance course at the technical college, evenings, the moment it's offered, even if I pay part of it. I'd ask the engineer who installs the robot loaders if I can watch. I'd push the union to make the company fund it. And I'd use AI to study, I already make it quiz me on the safety rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. A bit scared about money, because a course and less overtime means tighter months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd pay part of a course. With nothing left at the end of the month, where does that money come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good question. I'd sell my bass, probably, the good one. It's worth a few months of course fees. Sofia would say don't, but it's been in the cupboard for three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The guys who won't touch a screen. There's Henrik on the next lathe, fifty-five, he says "I don't trust it" about the phone, the chatbot, the new gauges. He's a better machinist than me. But I think they'd keep me and not him, and that's not fair.

S1.say: Robots are coming, and the question is whether workers get trained to run them or get thrown out. Unions should demand training budgets and a share of the gains.
S1.think: This could be good for me if I move fast, because someone has to program and look after the robot loaders. The risk is the company hires a technician from outside instead of training someone like me.
S1.do: Signs up for an evening robotics maintenance course and asks the installing engineer if he can watch. Pushes the union for company funding, uses AI to study, and would sell his bass to cover fees.
S1.feel: Mostly excited, with some fear about tighter months.
S1.quote: He's a better machinist than me. But I think they'd keep me and not him, and that's not fair.
S1.fieldNote: Rafael sees an opening and would move first, even selling his bass to pay for a course. Being adaptive makes him calm despite thin savings. What stood out was his discomfort that he'd be kept over a better machinist just for using screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Wow. Okay. So even the robot loaders I want to fix would fix themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for the biggest public policy fight in our lifetime: tax the machines, share the wealth, basic income for everybody. I'd be in the streets and I'd be organising, not just posting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, being quick with tech doesn't save me here, and that's a strange feeling for me. If it does everything better and cheaper, my head start is worth maybe six months. And we've got no savings, so six months is all it has to be worth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grab whatever paid work stays human the longest, maybe installing and setting up robots for other factories, because in the rush someone has to bolt them down. I'd cut everything: the car goes, we use the bus, Sofia and I cancel the phones down to the cheapest plans. I'd get very involved in the union and in any campaign for a basic income. And I'd still use AI every day, to find work and fill in forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but busy. I deal with fear by doing things, so I'd be doing a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd install robots for other factories. Isn't that helping the thing that takes everyone's jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I thought about that as I said it. But if it's coming in two years anyway, I'd rather be paid during the change than stand outside with a sign and no money. I can do both, I can bolt it down in the day and march at the weekend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Nico and Clara?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the truth, simply: papa's job is changing, we'll be fine, we'll do some things differently. Nico would ask if the robot is nice. Clara would ask if we can still have pizza on Fridays.

S2.say: This is the biggest public policy fight of our lifetime: tax the machines, share the wealth, basic income for everyone. I'd be organising in the streets, not just posting.
S2.think: Being quick with tech doesn't save me here, and that's a strange feeling. My head start is worth maybe six months, and with no savings six months is all it can be worth.
S2.do: Takes work installing and setting up robots for other factories while it lasts, and sells the car to use the bus while cutting phone plans. Organises in the union and basic income campaigns, and uses AI to find work and fill in forms.
S2.feel: Scared but busy, handling fear by doing things.
S2.quote: I can bolt it down in the day and march at the weekend.
S2.fieldNote: Rafael noticed his own contradiction as he spoke: installing the robots that take jobs while campaigning against job loss. He accepts it because money is too thin to stand aside. Being adaptive keeps him active, but he admits his head start barely counts here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough to do something real. Not enough to relax.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty for governments to prepare, so if they don't, it's a choice. Fund retraining, write rules on how fast firms can cut jobs, start the basic income pilots now. I'd say it at the union and I'd write to my representative, probably with the chatbot's help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd use the five years to get into robot maintenance properly and build up some money while it's still a job. I don't think it lasts forever. But five years of better pay could finally give us a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd start the robotics maintenance diploma part-time and try to get moved to the robot cell in the other hall. Any extra pay goes straight into savings, I'd set up an automatic transfer so I can't touch it. I'd stay in the union and push the campaign. We'd hold off on any big spending, like the bigger car Sofia wants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but mostly focused. I like having a clear target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the robot maintenance job won't last forever. What comes after it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know. Maybe nothing, maybe a basic income, maybe something nobody's thought of yet. I'm not going to pretend I know what work looks like in 2035.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Sofia wants a bigger car. How does that conversation go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly at first. She'd say I always have a plan that needs us to wait. And she's right, I had one with the band too. But this time I'd show her the numbers, the transfer every month, and that usually works with her.

S3.say: Five years is plenty for governments to prepare, so not preparing is a choice. Fund retraining, set rules on job cuts and start basic income pilots now.
S3.think: I'd use the five years to get properly into robot maintenance and build up money while it's still a job. It won't last forever, but five years of better pay could finally give us a cushion.
S3.do: Starts a part-time robotics maintenance diploma and asks to move to the robot cell. Sets up an automatic savings transfer for any extra pay, stays active in the union and campaign, and puts off buying a bigger car.
S3.feel: Mostly focused, with some unease underneath.
S3.quote: I'm not going to pretend I know what work looks like in 2035.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives Rafael a clear target and he becomes noticeably calmer and more organised. He's honest that his plan is a bridge, not an answer. Sofia's comment about his plans needing them to wait hints at a history of hopes that didn't pay off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be fifty-three. The kids would be twenty and seventeen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is the best chance we'll ever get to do this fairly, so let's not waste it. Public ownership of some of it, a basic income, free retraining. I'd say it everywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, ten years is almost a whole career in robot maintenance. That's enough to pay down a lot of the mortgage and save. The end point still worries me, because at fifty-three I'm not starting again easily. But I'd go in with something behind me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the diploma, get into maintenance, and maybe in a few years move to the company that makes the robots, because the makers will need people longest. I'd overpay the mortgage a little every month. I'd talk with the kids about what they study. And I'd be in the politics of it, the union and the campaigns.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. Uneasy about the end, but it's far enough that I can plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Nico about what to study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say learn to work with these tools, every day, like I did, and pick something where people need to trust a person. But honestly, I don't know. In ten years even my advice will be old.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you could ask the government for one thing in this ten-year picture, what would it be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Free retraining for adults with a wage while you do it. Not a loan, a wage. I'd have done it at forty if I could have afforded to stop working.

S4.say: A decade is the best chance we'll ever get to do this fairly, so let's not waste it. I'd push for some public ownership, a basic income and free retraining.
S4.think: Ten years is almost a whole career in robot maintenance, enough to pay down the mortgage and save. The end point still worries me at fifty-three, but I'd go in with something behind me.
S4.do: Completes the diploma, moves into maintenance and later aims for a robot maker. Overpays the mortgage a little each month, guides the kids' study choices and stays active in union campaigns.
S4.feel: Mostly okay, with unease about the end point.
S4.quote: Not a loan, a wage. I'd have done it at forty if I could have afforded to stop working.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years makes Rafael's adaptability pay off in money, not just skills. He still doesn't pretend to know how it ends. His one request, a wage while retraining, comes straight from his own experience of being unable to afford to stop.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Being quick doesn't help if there's no time and no money. What would help is a wage while you retrain, and a basic income that's ready before the jobs go, not after.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask people what they'd do if they didn't have to worry about money. I'd fix things and play music. I think most people still want to be useful, AGI or not.

headlineQuote: Being quick doesn't help if there's no time and no money.
portrait: Rafael is a forty-three-year-old former bar worker and bass player, two years into running CNC lathes at a car parts plant. He uses a chatbot every day to learn the machines and sees robot maintenance as his way up, even if it means selling his bass to pay for a course. He leans left and is angrier about how profits are shared than about the technology. Calm in the slower pictures, he becomes anxious with two years' warning, admitting that his head start is worth little with no savings.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because being quick with tech doesn't help when there's no time and no money.
whatWouldHelp: A wage while adults retrain, and a basic income set up before the jobs go rather than after.
